title: The One With Joeys New Brain

jokes.text: Ross tears up / gets emotional when Monica says the word 'wedding'
jokes.setup: Monica says 'wedding' in a neutral, planning context
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately gets emotional and choked up at just hearing the word, implying he's been through so many failed marriages/relationships
jokes.explanation: Classic character-specific joke that only works for Ross — a man on his third marriage who gets weepy at the mere mention of the word 'wedding.' Strong character integration and economy; the joke lands entirely on a single word trigger.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, I know. It's just... the word 'wedding.' Even saying it makes me uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I've been to three of them in the last year, and I'm not ready to think about another one.

jokes.text: Monica asks Ross, 'Do you think you could get through a poem?' after he breaks down at the word 'wedding'
jokes.setup: Ross volunteers enthusiastically to read a poem at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Monica undercuts his offer by pointedly questioning whether he can even get through it without crying
jokes.explanation: Tight callback that immediately pays off the previous joke. Monica's dry skepticism is well-earned and funny precisely because it's so reasonable given what just happened.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you think you can handle reading a poem at the wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A short one.

jokes.text: Chandler reacts to 'Too?' implying he already assumed he had something planned
jokes.setup: Monica says she has 'something else planned' for Chandler, but he responds 'too' as if he expected to be included
jokes.punchline: Monica catches his 'too' and realizes he thought he already had a role; she's keeping it secret ('on the Q.T.')
jokes.explanation: A mild joke about Chandler's obliviousness to his own role. Functional but not particularly sharp or character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I hope so. Maybe next week you'll tell me you're keeping something 'on the down low,' and the week after that you'll start saying '23 skidoo.'

jokes.text: 'Whatever it is, I hope it involves winking.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is told there's a secret plan for him at the wedding
jokes.punchline: His only wish is that it involves winking — a completely arbitrary and absurd preference
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed absurdist one-liner. The specificity of 'winking' makes it funnier than a generic answer would. Good economy — lands fast.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I got great news! I'm coming out of a coma!

jokes.text: Joey announces his character is coming out of a coma AND getting a new brain
jokes.setup: Joey excitedly says his character is coming out of his coma — positive news
jokes.punchline: He adds that he's also getting a NEW BRAIN — a brain transplant — escalating the absurdity of soap opera plotting
jokes.explanation: Classic soap opera absurdity gag — the coma recovery is already a cliché, so piling on a brain transplant escalates it perfectly. Joey's earnestness selling it as great news enhances the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm getting a new brain.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A brain transplant? Joey, that's a major surgical procedure. Do you understand the risks involved?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, I know.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I have to say, this might be the best thing that's ever happened to you. Finally, a chance for some real cognitive improvement.

jokes.text: 'So great things are happening at work and in your personal life.'
jokes.setup: Joey is thrilled about getting a brain transplant on a soap opera
jokes.punchline: Rachel responds with a perfectly dry, almost HR-speak summary treating it as a normal career update
jokes.explanation: Sharp deadpan delivery that derives its humor from treating something insane as mundane. Good economy — the line is short and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Brain transplants are ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, that's ridiculous? Your dry spell is ridiculous!

jokes.text: 'It's ridiculous.' / 'It's ridiculous that you haven't had sex in three and a half months.'
jokes.setup: Ross says the brain transplant storyline is 'ridiculous'
jokes.punchline: Rachel hijacks the word 'ridiculous' to redirect it at Ross's sex life — specifically three and a half months of celibacy
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection: Ross's 'ridiculous' is clearly about soap operas, then Rachel pivots it to something personal and embarrassing about Ross. The specificity of 'three and a half months' (not 'three' or 'a few') is a great comedy detail — precise enough to feel real. Very economical structure. Close to an 8-level joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Look, it's not that I'm not trying. It's just that winter is a nightmare for dating in the city. Everyone's bundled up, walking fast, heads down. There's no eye contact, no opportunities for organic meetings.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And spring? Forget about it. Everyone's on their way somewhere. Summer, they're all traveling. Fall, they're back in relationships from summer. The pedestrian traffic patterns are completely against me.

jokes.text: 'It's winter. There are fewer people on the street.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just mocked Ross for not having sex in three and a half months
jokes.punchline: Ross explains his drought by referencing seasonal pedestrian traffic — implying he picks up women on the street, which is both pathetic and bizarre
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The logic is completely absurd but delivered as a completely sincere explanation, which makes it funnier. It implies Ross is out there picking up women on the sidewalk like a predator, which is both a self-own and an oddly specific justification. High originality, great economy, very quotable. Earns a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. So every time she throws a drink in someone's face, she's never worried about the dry cleaning bill?

jokes.text: 'She is so good at throwing drinks in people's faces. I don't think I've ever seen her finish a beverage.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Phoebe gush about their favorite Days of Our Lives character, Cecilia Monroe/Jessica Lockhart
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's tribute devolves into the specific observation that the character has never finished a drink due to constant face-throwing
jokes.explanation: Clever deconstruction of the soap opera drink-throw trope. 'I don't think I've ever seen her finish a beverage' is a great comedy observation — it takes a trope and extends it to its logical, absurd conclusion. Good economy and genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no, no! That doesn't make any sense! You can't just transplant someone's brain into another person's body!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? You're a scientist guy!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a paleontologist, Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right, so you know about science stuff. So what's the big deal?

jokes.text: 'Why is this so hard for you to get? I thought you were a scientist.'
jokes.setup: Ross, an actual scientist (paleontologist), struggles to understand how a soap opera brain transplant storyline works
jokes.punchline: Joey (the actor on the soap) condescends to Ross about not grasping the fictional science
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy — Joey ironically deploying Ross's own credential against him, as if Ross's scientific knowledge should help him understand soap opera pseudoscience. The reversal is sharp and character-specific. Joey's cluelessness about what 'scientist' means is the core of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why do you think he's gay?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He's a interior decorator.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He's really good at it.

jokes.text: Rachel explains why she thinks a man is gay: 'Mainly because he's kissing that other guy.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks Rachel why she thinks a man across the coffee shop is gay
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'sophisticated' answer is simply: he's kissing another man — delivered as if it's an insightful observation
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection/anticlimax joke — the setup implies Rachel will give a nuanced or perceptive reason, and instead she states the most obvious possible evidence. Well-structured and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Look, there's a different guy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, he's bald! That means he's either a thug or a really successful businessman. There's no in-between.

jokes.text: 'Oh, no, not that guy there. That guy right there.' (Phoebe was pointing at a different man entirely)
jokes.setup: Rachel gives her gay-detecting answer confidently
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reveals she was asking about a different man — making Rachel's answer irrelevant and her confidence misplaced
jokes.explanation: A quick double-beat that makes the previous joke land harder by pulling the rug out from under Rachel. Good tight structure — both jokes work together better than either does alone.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! I know! We could see if he likes showtunes!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No wait, that doesn't work. Joey likes showtunes.

jokes.text: 'Oh, yeah, he's too cute to be straight.'
jokes.setup: Now looking at the correct man, Rachel and Phoebe assess him
jokes.punchline: Rachel's assessment is based purely on him being too good-looking — implying straight men can't be that attractive
jokes.explanation: A familiar observational joke about the 'too cute to be straight' stereotype. Gets a chuckle but isn't particularly original. The attitude fits Rachel's character but doesn't transcend the cliché.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They could turn the phone into lost and found.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We could use someone's phone for international calls and just tell them we're checking on friends.

jokes.text: 'Knockers will help us figure it out.' (a man approaches with notably large chest)
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Rachel are debating the man's sexuality
jokes.punchline: Phoebe references 'Knockers' — presumably a person or nickname — to settle the debate; the visual of a large man arriving is implied
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing — implies they have a friend/regular who can read these situations. Without the visual it's somewhat flat on the page, but the implied physical gag carries it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I found this phone on the street and I'm like, what if the owner and I meet and it's like fate? Like, we lock eyes across a crowded room and—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's called stealing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, it's called destiny.

jokes.text: 'All right, straight. And not subtle.'
jokes.setup: 'Knockers' has assessed the man's sexuality
jokes.punchline: The verdict is delivered in two crisp words — 'straight. And not subtle' — implying the man was visibly, aggressively heterosexual
jokes.explanation: Great economy — 'And not subtle' is a funny addendum that implies something visually hyper-masculine about the man. The brevity and confidence of the delivery is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, weren't you just on a date three days ago?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, that wasn't a date. That was just casual sex.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So what's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, a date is when you go out and do something nice with someone. Casual sex is just... casual sex.

jokes.text: Rachel suggests they call China on the found cell phone 'to see how those guys are doing'
jokes.setup: A man has left his cell phone behind at the coffee shop
jokes.punchline: Rachel suggests using it to call China — not for any practical reason, just vague curiosity about how 'those guys' are doing
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist joke with real charm. 'See how those guys are doing' is a funny vague reason — it sounds like Rachel genuinely has mild, friendly curiosity about the whole country. Character-consistent with her oblivious self-absorption.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I thought I'd never love again!

jokes.text: Phoebe's romantic fantasy about finding love through a stranger's cell phone — 'kind of like a fairy tale for the digital age'
jokes.setup: Phoebe imagines that if the man calls his phone, she'll answer, they'll talk, fall in love, and it will be a great story
jokes.punchline: She calls it 'a fairy tale for the digital age' — framing an absurd meet-cute scheme as profound and romantic
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — the romantic idealism and earnestness is perfectly in character. 'Digital age' as a descriptor for such a low-tech scheme is funny. The character specificity elevates what would otherwise be a mild joke.

jokes.text: 'Phoebe, you had a date three days ago.' / 'That wasn't a date. That was friends getting together and having sex.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe claims she hasn't been on a date in so long, to justify claiming the phone
jokes.punchline: When Rachel points out she had a date three days ago, Phoebe's clarification redefines it as simply 'friends getting together and having sex'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Phoebe's claim is questioned, and her clarification creates an entirely new absurdity. 'Friends getting together and having sex' is a brilliantly Phoebe-specific distinction — deeply weird, delivered with total sincerity. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: I didn't mean to kill him! It was an accident!

dialogue.speaker: Other character
dialogue.line: Well, you're an accident.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, and until now, I didn't think I would love again.' (Rachel, one week after breaking up with Tag)
jokes.setup: Rachel argues she should get the phone because she broke up with Tag a week ago
jokes.punchline: She claims that until seeing this stranger, she 'didn't think she would love again' — an absurd overstatement after just one week
jokes.explanation: A quick, solid joke about Rachel's dramatic self-pity. The one-week detail from earlier makes the overstatement land. Fits her character well but isn't exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was a real slap! My face is killing me!

jokes.text: Rachel and Phoebe race to grab the phone — Phoebe gets it; 'Aha! Too slow!' then Rachel grabs it back: 'Aha! Too cocky.'
jokes.setup: They can't agree on who should get the phone, so they decide to let fate decide
jokes.punchline: What begins as a moment of fate becomes a physical scuffle; Phoebe gloats and Rachel immediately steals it back, delivering a perfect comeback
jokes.explanation: 'Too cocky' as a one-word callback to 'too slow' is a beautifully economical structure. The physical comedy escalates quickly and the verbal payoff lands cleanly. The rhythm between the two lines is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, it's me! From yesterday's scene?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're a real person!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm an actor.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: I thought you were just a prop they moved around.

jokes.text: Soap opera dialogue: 'What are you going to do, kill him? Like you did Charles?' / 'That was an accident.' / 'And so were you.'
jokes.setup: Two characters in a soap opera argue dramatically
jokes.punchline: 'And so were you' — a devastating personal attack delivered as a soap opera zinger
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp piece of scripted soap melodrama. 'And so were you' as a retort is structurally elegant — it uses a previous word ('accident') and weaponizes it personally. Would work as a standalone comedy line in any context. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Which one of you told Joey I was leaving?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Okay, tall one, was it you?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Bald one?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Jewish one?

jokes.text: 'That was a great scene. That slap looked so real. How do you do that?' / 'Oh, just years of experience.' / 'Can I get some ice here?!'
jokes.setup: Joey compliments Cecilia on the realistically-looking slap in the scene they just filmed
jokes.punchline: She says 'years of experience' — implying it's performance craft — but the immediate 'Can I get some ice here?!' reveals she actually did slap him for real
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed three-part joke. The setup (compliment), the misdirection (her modest professional answer), and the punchline (someone is screaming for ice) all click together cleanly. The final line recontextualizes her earlier gloating about slapping as not performance skill, but actual aggression. Earned and clever.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you'd want to do the name game if it worked out for you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Rachel, ratchet. You'd be all about it.

jokes.text: Cecilia mistakes Joey for a dying fan she was scheduled to hug
jokes.setup: Joey approaches Cecilia Monroe to introduce himself as a co-star
jokes.punchline: She assumes he must be the dying fan she's supposed to hug, because she can't conceive that anyone approaching her with admiration is a colleague
jokes.explanation: A great character introduction joke that immediately establishes Cecilia's self-importance. She has such a high opinion of herself that a co-star's admiration can only make sense if they're a dying fan. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, Phoebe, didn't you use that same story to get out of paying for coffee last week?

jokes.text: Joey tells Cecilia he's getting her brain — revealing to her that she's being written off the show
jokes.setup: Joey naively mentions he's getting 'her brain' in the transplant, expecting she already knows
jokes.punchline: Cecilia has absolutely no idea she's being written off the show — Joey has accidentally revealed it
jokes.explanation: A cringe comedy moment with real escalation potential. Joey's obliviousness accidentally blowing up Cecilia's career security is well-executed — the horror of her 'I'm leaving the show?' is played perfectly against Joey's confusion.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have a deep spiritual connection with Yoga.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I wish it was Yogurt. That's more my speed.

jokes.text: 'Who told you that? Was it bald or was it tall?' (Cecilia's frantic question about which writer told Joey)
jokes.setup: Cecilia is reeling from learning she's being written off the show and demands to know which writer told Joey
jokes.punchline: Her question classifies the writers only by physical description ('bald or tall') — implying she doesn't know their names, only their appearance
jokes.explanation: Funny character detail — Cecilia is so dismissive of the writers that she can't be bothered to know their names. The binary 'bald or tall' is a funny specific choice. Character comedy that layers onto her diva persona.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Who has Barneys on speed dial?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That would be me.

jokes.text: 'You know, it doesn't matter, because it is not true.' Then immediately: 'And if it were true, how dare you come to me and ask for tips!'
jokes.setup: Cecilia denies the rumor about being written off
jokes.punchline: In the same breath she hypothetically rages about what she'd do IF it were true — betraying that she suspects it might be
jokes.explanation: Classic comic contradiction — a character denies something then immediately argues the hypothetical of it being true. The transition ('And if it WERE true') reveals her panic beneath the denial. Well-structured and character-specific to a diva actress.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What is that noise?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That would be the sound of a thousand cats being murdered.

jokes.text: 'Or we can decide by whoever's name is closer to the word phone.'
jokes.setup: Rachel proposes using the man's speed dial contacts to determine who's more compatible with him
jokes.punchline: Phoebe counter-proposes a completely arbitrary linguistic proximity rule that obviously favors her ('Phoebe' rhymes more with 'phone')
jokes.explanation: A great Phoebe joke — she proposes a totally made-up fairness rule that transparently benefits her. The logic is absurd but delivered earnestly. 'Phone' and 'Phoebe' don't even sound that alike, which makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why is your family Scottish?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why is YOUR family the way it is?

jokes.text: 'Fine. But I bet you'd be singing a different tune if we were fighting over a ratchet.'
jokes.setup: Rachel rejects Phoebe's name-proximity rule
jokes.punchline: Phoebe threatens that the same logic would favor Rachel if they were fighting over a 'ratchet' — a completely non-sequitur object
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best Phoebe lines in the series. The substitution of 'ratchet' for 'phone' is perfectly absurd — a ratchet has zero relationship to anything happening, yet Phoebe's logic is internally consistent. 'Singing a different tune' as a phrase combined with 'ratchet' is a great unexpected collision. High originality, strong economy, and deeply Phoebe-specific. Earns the 8+ score.

jokes.text: 'First name on the speed dial is Mom.' / 'Oh. I lost my mom to suicide.'
jokes.setup: They're evaluating the man's speed dial contacts to determine compatibility
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately deploys her dead mother (by suicide) as a compatibility point — using genuine tragedy as a tactical weapon
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny — Phoebe uses a genuinely sad biographical detail as a competitive advantage in a trivial argument. The casualness with which she drops 'I lost my mom to suicide' as a logical point is perfectly Phoebe. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait... I think I hear 'Smooth Criminal'!

jokes.text: 'No way. You can't use that to get the cute guy AND the last blueberry muffin.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to use her dead mother by suicide as a trump card
jokes.punchline: Rachel reveals Phoebe already used this card today to get the last blueberry muffin — implying a whole history of manipulative grief deployment
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the stronger Friends jokes overall. The escalation is what makes it exceptional — it's not just that Phoebe uses her mother's suicide as a tactic, it's that she's ALREADY used it today, and she used it to get a MUFFIN. The specificity of 'last blueberry muffin' is genius. This reveals an entire character history in one line, and the word 'and' (as if the cute guy and the muffin are equivalent) adds further comedy. Highly quotable, perfectly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, Phoebe, if you don't have my phone, then how do you explain this?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm calling it right now.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! That's not your phone. That's just my Walkman. My Walkman sounds exactly like a phone.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, it's weird.

jokes.text: 'Did I use that already today? I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just exposed that Phoebe used her dead mother trick earlier for a muffin
jokes.punchline: Phoebe doesn't deny it — she checks in with mild embarrassment about overuse ('today'), not about the fact of using it at all
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The qualifier 'today' is what makes it exceptional — she's not apologizing for manipulating people with her mother's death, only for the frequency. The implication that tomorrow is fair game is hilarious. 'I'm sorry' as genuine remorse about the schedule, not the act, is beautifully deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Rachel? Oh, she's not here right now. Can I take a message?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hold on, let me transfer you to her.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hi, this is Rachel speaking.

jokes.text: 'I do yoga. That's one for me.' / 'Oh, all right. Oh, so close. If only it said yogurt.'
jokes.setup: They're tallying speed-dial contacts against their interests. Phoebe scores 'Yoga' as a point for herself
jokes.punchline: Rachel laments that she almost scored too — if only the contact said 'yogurt' instead of 'yoga'
jokes.explanation: A charming absurdist Rachel joke. 'Yogurt' as a parallel to 'yoga' is funny because it's similar-sounding but completely different — and eating yogurt is nowhere near a lifestyle passion. The earnestness of her near-miss sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I need to be alone when he comes over.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, my mom killed herself, so...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Phoebe, I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it's only the first time today I've used that.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I win. He's got Barneys on his speed dial.' / 'You don't know it's Barneys the store. That could be his friend or a bar.' / 'Who has Barneys the store on their speed dial? His new girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe claims victory because 'Barneys' is on the speed dial, implying the high-end store
jokes.punchline: Rachel argues it could be a person or a bar, but Phoebe's rejoinder — 'Who has Barneys the store on their speed dial? His new girlfriend' — is a perfect mic-drop
jokes.explanation: A clever comedic argument where both sides are funny. Rachel's pedantic objection is funny, but Phoebe's rebuke is sharp and conclusive. 'His new girlfriend' as the answer sets up the eventual plot beat with great comic confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, how old are you?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 15? So in 3 years you'll be 18...

jokes.text: "You don't know it's Barneys the store. That could be his friend's house or a bar... Who has Barneys the store on their speed dial? His new girlfriend."
jokes.setup: Phoebe claims victory because Barneys is on the speed dial; Rachel disputes it
jokes.punchline: After Rachel argues it could be a friend or bar, she defeats herself by suggesting it could be 'his new girlfriend' — implying the girlfriend's name is Barneys, which is absurd
jokes.explanation: Solid exchange. The escalating possibilities for what 'Barneys' could mean, capped with Rachel's self-undermining 'his new girlfriend,' shows good structural awareness. The punchline is unexpected but logical in a funny way.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Jessica doesn't have an English accent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I thought I was doing one!

jokes.text: Monica and Chandler hear a horrific noise and Monica says 'I think it's the Dying Cat Parade.'
jokes.setup: An awful noise is heard coming from across the street; Monica and Chandler try to identify it
jokes.punchline: Monica's conclusion is that it must be the 'Dying Cat Parade' — a fake-sounding but somehow plausible New York City event
jokes.explanation: 'Dying Cat Parade' is a great comic coinage — specific enough to be visual and silly enough to be absurd. It also works as a New York gag: in New York, any bizarre event is plausible. Memorable phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I can do an English accent!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great, Joe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm adding it to my résumé right now.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you just discovered you can do it five seconds ago.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So? I'm fluent!

jokes.text: Monica and Chandler realize the terrible noise is Ross playing bagpipes — 'The thing that Ross was gonna do at our wedding'
jokes.setup: They've been debating what Ross's secret plan for the wedding is; they hear a terrible noise
jokes.punchline: The noise IS Ross's contribution — he's been practicing bagpipes and that's what he wants to play at the wedding
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the mystery setup from the opening. The reveal that the horrific noise is Ross practicing bagpipes is well-executed because we've been dreading it right along with Monica and Chandler. The structure of building dread via the sound sells the joke before anyone speaks.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: By Vikings.

jokes.text: 'Unbelievable. Why is your family Scottish?' / 'Why is your family Ross?'
jokes.setup: Chandler blames Monica's Scottish heritage for inviting this problem
jokes.punchline: Monica deflects by blaming Chandler's family for producing Ross — a completely illogical but perfect retort
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest exchanges in the episode. 'Why is your family Scottish?' is already funny; 'Why is your family Ross?' is exceptional. The parallel structure makes the illogic of the retort land perfectly — Chandler's question about ethnicity is met with an existential complaint about his family producing a specific person. Perfect economy (four words), high quotability, great character specificity. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What are Swedish people famous for?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Meatballs.

jokes.text: 'It'll be like when he rapped at my bat mitzvah.'
jokes.setup: Monica is horrified about Ross playing bagpipes at the wedding
jokes.punchline: She references Ross rapping at her bat mitzvah as a comparable disaster — establishing a whole pattern of Ross ruining milestone events with musical performances
jokes.explanation: A great background detail that gets a big laugh through implication alone. We don't need to see Ross rapping at a bat mitzvah — the image is instantly fully-formed and hilarious. Establishes a pattern of behavior that makes the current crisis funnier. High character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because they sound like a dying animal, Ross. A dying animal that nobody likes.

jokes.text: Ross's argument: 'You haven't heard me play. You've heard me PRACTICE.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler say they've heard him play and they hate it
jokes.punchline: Ross insists there's a meaningful distinction between his practicing (horrible) and his actual performance — implying his performance will be better, which the audience finds delusional
jokes.explanation: A solid character joke about Ross's delusional self-confidence. The practice/performance distinction is a believably Ross-like rationalization. Works well in context but is a familiar comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm going to play something that's going to change your minds about me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a Scottish celebration song. A Ceilidh-bration!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh no.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm playing 'Celebration'!

jokes.text: Ross teases 'I'll bet there'll be a wee bit of celebration' — implying he'll play 'Celebration' by Kool and the Gang on bagpipes
jokes.setup: Ross says he won't reveal the song but gives a hint
jokes.punchline: 'A wee bit of celebration' — 'wee' as a Scottish word + 'Celebration' as the song title — a double pun that's also a terrible preview of what's coming
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-layered pun that also functions as dramatic irony — Monica and Chandler know exactly what song it is and are already dreading it. 'Wee' doing double duty as both Scottish and a size-qualifier is clever.

jokes.text: Very slow realization of 'Celebration' buried in the horrendous bagpipe playing — 'Wait. If you listen very carefully... I think it's Celebration by Kool and the Gang.'
jokes.setup: Monica declares the bagpipe noise 'just noise,' 'not even a song'
jokes.punchline: Chandler, listening intently, eventually picks out 'Celebration' in the cacophony — confirming Ross's hint while emphasizing how bad his playing is
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the hint from moments ago. The joke is partly structural — Chandler has to strain to identify it — which implies just how garbled Ross's playing is. Good running gag setup for the bagpipe subplot.

jokes.text: Phoebe pretends to 'show Rachel the features' of her 'new ringing handbag' — while Rachel's stolen phone rings inside it
jokes.setup: Rachel suspects Phoebe stole the phone back and suggests calling it to prove it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe — knowing the phone is in her bag — spins this into a demonstration of her 'new ringing handbag' as the phone rings inside it
jokes.explanation: A clever bit of physical misdirection. Phoebe's attempt to convert damning evidence into a product demonstration is a creative and character-consistent escape attempt. The 'ringing handbag' as a quick cover is very Phoebe — she commits to absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Your acting was amazing. You know, you're really talented.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And you look great in that dress.

jokes.text: 'Hello. Yes, hi, is Rachel there?' / 'Yes, she is. Just one moment please.' / 'It's for me!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has called the phone as a trap; Phoebe answers on the stolen phone pretending it's her own
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls Rachel on the stolen phone as a fake call, then hands it to herself, declaring 'It's for me!' — a performative act of brass-faced theft
jokes.explanation: Fantastic escalation of the phone bit. Phoebe's decision to call Rachel on the phone she's denying stealing, then triumphantly declare 'It's for me!' is a brilliantly audacious move. The gall of it makes it very funny. 'That is damning evidence' as Rachel's response seals it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Does she put her hands on faces because she's passionate?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Actually, it's a selfish camera trick. She does it so the camera focuses on her hands instead of her face.

jokes.text: 'That is damning evidence.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just answered a call from Rachel on the supposedly non-existent stolen phone, then declared it's for her
jokes.punchline: Rachel's flat assessment: 'That is damning evidence' — treating the absurd situation with mock-judicial seriousness
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan button on the previous joke. The faux-legal language applied to a petty friend squabble is very funny. Great economy — four words do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, hi! We've been waiting for—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How long were we arguing?

jokes.text: Phoebe gives out Rachel's home address to the stranger over the phone, planning her date at Rachel's apartment
jokes.setup: Phoebe is setting up a date with the phone's owner using the stolen phone
jokes.punchline: She confidently gives out Rachel's apartment address as her own for the date — right in front of Rachel
jokes.explanation: A solid escalation joke — Phoebe's audacity in giving out Rachel's address is funny but the punchline (Rachel pointing out she'll be there) is the real payoff to come.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, this is actually better. At least he shows up on time.

jokes.text: 'You do know that I will be here when he comes over.' / 'How will you know what time to come over?' / 'You just said it.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just given Rachel's address and arranged a time — right in front of Rachel
jokes.punchline: Phoebe asks how Rachel would know when to show up, then realizes she literally just said the time out loud
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed self-undermining joke. Phoebe's moment of 'gotcha' is immediately deflated by Rachel's simple, accurate reply. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They don't make them like that anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, they do. I'm one of them.

jokes.text: 'You know, to think about my mom and her suicide.' / 'Oh, Phoebe!' / 'What? That's the first time today.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to make Rachel feel guilty about being at the apartment by invoking her mother's suicide
jokes.punchline: When Rachel protests, Phoebe points out 'That's the first time today' — confirming the earlier joke about daily ration of using it
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback that makes the running gag even better. 'That's the first time today' confirms that Phoebe has an internal quota system for deploying her mother's suicide. The implication that she's rationing it is funnier than any single use of the joke. Strong economy and excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: You own the room.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I do? What's the square footage? Is it rent-controlled?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: No, Joey, I mean you command the room. You have presence.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh. That's way less valuable.

jokes.text: 'So you like the nachos, huh? Myself, I'm partial to...' / 'I'm 16.' / 'See you in 2003.'
jokes.setup: Joey (at the DOOL studio craft services or similar) is chatting up what he thinks is a potential date
jokes.punchline: She reveals she's 16; Joey immediately calculates when she'll be legal ('See you in 2003') and walks off — treating the situation as simply a scheduling matter
jokes.explanation: A great Joey joke that walks the dark edge. The horror is that Joey's response isn't anger or shame — it's a calendar calculation. 'See you in 2003' treats statutory law as simply a scheduling inconvenience. Perfectly in character and very funny. The casualness of departure sells it. High character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: So Monica is your roommate? That explains all the women's underwear in the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, that's... that's exactly what it is.

jokes.text: Joey does Cecilia's character voice with a full English accent: 'Jessica Lockhart will never step foot in this place again!'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to capture the essence of Cecilia's character for the brain transplant storyline
jokes.punchline: His attempt is in a full English accent — which is completely wrong for the character and surprises everyone including him
jokes.explanation: A reliable physical comedy bit — Joey's unexpected English accent when trying to imitate an American character. The setup of his sincere effort makes the wrong accent funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Will you slap me?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: I can't. I have legal restrictions on slapping fans.

jokes.text: 'But Jessica doesn't have an English accent.' / 'I can do an English accent?'
jokes.setup: Cecilia points out that Joey's accent is completely wrong for the character
jokes.punchline: Joey's reaction is not embarrassment but delight — he's just discovered he can do an English accent, treating it as a bonus skill
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Joey moments. His pivot from 'I failed at this task' to 'I discovered a talent!' is perfectly in character. 'I can do an English accent?' as a question is exactly right — he's genuinely learning this about himself for the first time. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? Your outfit is terrible and you have no sense of style.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: I appreciate your feedback, but I'm going to maintain professional boundaries here.

jokes.text: 'That baby's going on my résumé.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just discovered he can do an English accent (which he actually could already do wrong)
jokes.punchline: He immediately announces he's adding it to his résumé — full commitment to treating a mediocre misdirected accent as a professional credential
jokes.explanation: A great button on the previous joke. Joey's self-delusion about his acting abilities is a core character trait, and 'That baby's going on my résumé' is a perfectly compressed expression of it. Very quotable, excellent economy, strong character integration. 'That baby' as a phrase adds to the charm.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: Jessica hates horses.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, the electric fence will create a new phobia.

jokes.text: Ross uses shortbread to try to soften Monica and Chandler to bagpipes — 'It's Scottish, like you are'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to get Monica to embrace their Scottish heritage and therefore embrace his bagpipe plan
jokes.punchline: He offers shortbread as a bribe to reconnect her with Scottish culture — a transparently manipulative and naive tactic
jokes.explanation: A mild joke that sets up the Scottish heritage conversation. Ross's naivety in thinking shortbread will help is mildly funny but not developed enough to get a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm imagining it. And it's not pretty. Actually, it's pretty great.

jokes.text: "Oh, no, thanks. I don't like anything from my Scottish heritage."
jokes.setup: Ross offers Monica shortbread on the basis of her Scottish heritage
jokes.punchline: Monica flatly rejects not just the shortbread but her entire Scottish heritage as something she doesn't like
jokes.explanation: Decent line — the categorical rejection of an entire heritage as a food preference is mildly funny. Establishes the comedic premise that Monica has no connection to her Scottish roots.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Monica's family was 'run out of Scotland by... Vikings'
jokes.setup: Ross is pushing Monica to reconnect with her Scottish heritage; Monica explains why the family doesn't
jokes.punchline: The family was run out by Vikings — a historically improbable, specific, and gloriously random explanation delivered as fact
jokes.explanation: The long pause before 'Vikings' is the joke — the absurdity of the specific historical detail as a family trauma. Delivered with the same gravity as a genuine family backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I'm playing Jessica, a neurosurgeon who just discovered that her brain was transplanted into the body of her evil twin sister!

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: *dramatic pause* And she's been living MY life for the past five years.

jokes.text: "Well, it's just that my entire family was run out of Scotland by... Vikings." (long pause before 'Vikings')
jokes.setup: Monica explains why she doesn't like her Scottish heritage
jokes.punchline: The explanation — family run out of Scotland by Vikings — is historically absurd (Vikings and Scots occupied Scotland in different eras), and the pause before 'Vikings' suggests even Monica isn't sure this is right
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist historical joke. The Viking detail is both historically questionable and charmingly specific. The implied pause before 'Vikings' (inferred from the transcript layout) suggests Monica herself isn't certain — which adds a layer of comedy. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: I was in a film festival in Guadalajara.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Guadalajara? Isn't that near LaGuardia?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: No, that's an airport in New York.

jokes.text: 'But, you know, Chandler's also half-Swedish. You know what the Swedish people are famous for? Sitting down and being quiet.'
jokes.setup: Ross continues pushing bagpipes via Scottish heritage; Monica tries to redirect to Chandler's Swedish side
jokes.punchline: She claims Swedes are famous for 'sitting down and being quiet' — an entirely fabricated cultural stereotype invented purely to argue against bagpipes
jokes.explanation: A great joke in Monica's voice — the Swedish 'sitting down and being quiet' is a perfectly specific anti-stereotype. It's not a real Swedish stereotype but it sounds like it could be one, and it's deployed with Monica's signature control-freak energy. The setup/payoff structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Own a few places? Like what, apartments?

dialogue.speaker: Cecilia
dialogue.line: No, Joey. It's about confidence. Own the room.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! OH! Right, right. Confidence. Got it.

jokes.text: "Were you the ones who called the cops?" "That's not really important right now."
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler confront Ross about playing bagpipes; Ross asks if they called the cops on him
jokes.punchline: Monica's non-answer — 'that's not really important right now' — is effectively a yes, confirming that his playing was bad enough to warrant police involvement
jokes.explanation: Solid deflection joke. Monica's diplomatic non-answer is an effective comedic device — it confirms the worst without saying it. The implication that Ross's practicing was so bad someone called the police adds to the running gag about the awfulness of his bagpipes.

jokes.text: 'Why not?' / 'Because we hate them.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks why bagpipes aren't appropriate for the wedding — expecting a cultural or logistical reason
jokes.punchline: Monica's answer is the simplest possible: 'Because we hate them' — cutting through all diplomatic hedging
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words do complete work. After all the diplomatic hedging and careful phrasing around Ross's feelings, Monica just says the truth directly. The bluntness after the buildup is the joke.

jokes.text: 'That's not true. Look at Angela Lansbur... Angelina Jolie.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to reassure Cecilia that an actress of her age can still find great work
jokes.punchline: He starts to name Angela Lansbury as an example of an older actress, then catches himself and pivots to Angelina Jolie — a much younger actress, undercutting his reassurance
jokes.explanation: A smart, well-constructed joke about Joey's sweet but oblivious bumbling. He starts to name the right person (an older successful actress) and then self-corrects in the wrong direction (to a 25-year-old). The mid-word pivot — 'Angela Lansbur...' to 'Angelina Jolie' — is the key comic beat. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Cecilia reveals she turned down Mexican cinema work and 'the landscape of Mexican cinema would be very different today'
jokes.setup: Cecilia reflects on opportunities she passed up while comfortable on the soap
jokes.punchline: She claims to have had a potentially transformative impact on Mexican cinema — a grandiose self-assessment delivered as simple fact
jokes.explanation: A great character bit that deepens Cecilia's delusion. Her casual claim to have almost transformed an entire national cinema is both funny and completely believable from this character. The specificity of 'Mexican cinema' is funnier than a vaguer claim would be.

jokes.text: Joey tells a crying Cecilia 'I'm also thinking, she is hot' — in a moment meant to be comforting
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to comfort Cecilia about being written off the show, saying he thinks she's a great actress
jokes.punchline: He adds that he's also thinking 'she is hot' — framing leering as a compliment and comfort
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — he thinks he's giving double praise (talent AND beauty) and doesn't understand why the second part might be inappropriate in a vulnerable moment. Character-specific and mildly funny, though it's a well-worn Joey move.

jokes.text: 'You think I'm hot?' / 'You own the room.'
jokes.setup: Joey calls Cecilia hot; she reacts with a pleased vanity response
jokes.punchline: Joey repurposes the acting coaching phrase 'you own the room' in this new context — she visibly snaps back into her confident persona through flattery
jokes.explanation: A clever repurposing of the acting coaching phrase in a romantic/flattery context. The double meaning works well — both as a seduction line and as a callback to the lesson. Cecilia's immediate transformation is the visual punchline.

jokes.text: Cecilia explains the 'hands on the face' technique is not about passion — 'it's because that way the camera only sees her'
jokes.setup: Joey asks if Cecilia's signature kiss technique (hands on the man's face) is because Jessica is so passionate
jokes.punchline: Cecilia deflates the romance entirely: it's a camera-blocking technique so the audience only sees her face, not her partner's
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. What looks like a passionate romantic gesture is revealed as a narcissistic camera-blocking technique. The reveal perfectly encapsulates Cecilia's entire character — it's all about her being seen. The structure is clean, the revelation is funny and surprising, and it's deeply character-specific. Earns a high score.

jokes.text: Joey and Cecilia's 'demonstration' kiss that goes on way too long — Chandler and Monica walk in mid-kiss
jokes.setup: Cecilia offers to demonstrate the kissing technique on Joey for his preparation
jokes.punchline: The kiss extends far past instructional necessity; Chandler and Monica walk in on them, clearly making it a romantic/personal kiss rather than professional
jokes.explanation: A classic 'caught in the act' visual comedy beat. The extended kiss is funny because of how long it must go on before the interruption. Not the most original gag but executed with good timing implied by the transcript.

jokes.text: 'Hey, hey!' — Chandler and Monica's interruption of the Joey/Cecilia kiss
jokes.setup: Joey and Cecilia have been kissing — presumably for far too long
jokes.punchline: Chandler and Monica's simultaneous 'Hey, hey!' is the reaction that confirms how inappropriate the scene has become
jokes.explanation: A functional reaction beat that punctuates the previous joke. Not particularly clever on its own, but it serves the scene rhythm.

jokes.text: 'Okay. Good luck explaining all the calls to China.'
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe argue about who answers the door to give back the cell phone
jokes.punchline: Rachel concedes the door to Phoebe but reminds her about the calls they made to China on the stolen phone
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the earlier China joke. The implication that they actually did call China is funnier than the original suggestion. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Wow, how long were we arguing for?' (after seeing the attractive Tom)
jokes.setup: An extremely attractive man walks in to pick up the phone
jokes.punchline: Rachel and Phoebe both stop arguing instantly, stunned — Rachel's question implies they both forgot about everything else
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny reaction to attraction overwhelming logic. The implied blank-out from seeing someone handsome is a recognizable and mildly funny gag.

jokes.text: "Can you believe this? We were waiting for a hot guy, and then an even hotter one shows up."
jokes.setup: An even more attractive man than expected shows up
jokes.punchline: The frank assessment of the situation — narrated as an extraordinary stroke of luck — is funny in its self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Light observational comedy. The direct narration of their luck is mildly funny but not especially crafted. Transitional joke.

jokes.text: 'They just don't make them like that anymore, you know?' / 'No, they do, but you just have to wait.'
jokes.setup: Both women are dazzled by Tom's attractiveness
jokes.punchline: Phoebe eulogizes attractive men as an extinct species; Rachel's response corrects her with weary romantic optimism
jokes.explanation: A mild, pleasant exchange. Phoebe's nostalgia for good-looking men is funny; Rachel's correction is wry. Neither line is exceptional but together they're a charming beat.

jokes.text: Cecilia Monroe arrives at Joey's apartment — Rachel launches into full fan-girl mode: 'Oh, Jessica Lockhart! In my apartment!'
jokes.setup: Joey has brought his soap opera co-star home; Rachel (who earlier said she'd never seen Jessica finish a beverage) encounters her idol in person
jokes.punchline: Rachel completely loses her composure, screaming 'Jessica Lockhart! In my apartment!' — unable to process that the character and the actress are different people
jokes.explanation: Funny callback to the earlier scene where Monica and Rachel gushed about the character. Rachel's inability to call the actress by her real name and instead calling her by the character name is a recognizable fan-behavior joke.

jokes.text: Monica rushes in screaming 'Monica!' after Rachel introduces her — Cecilia assumes Monica is the name of the roommate and responds 'That explains all the women's underwear.'
jokes.setup: Rachel yells 'Monica!' to get her roommate's attention; Cecilia interprets 'Monica' as an introduction
jokes.punchline: Cecilia's response — 'That explains all the women's underwear' — is simultaneously a reasonable inference and an absurd non-sequitur about Monica's presence explaining the underwear
jokes.explanation: A quick, mildly funny misunderstanding gag. 'That explains all the women's underwear' as a response is funny because it implies Cecilia had genuinely been puzzled by the underwear — suggesting she thought Joey lived there alone.

jokes.text: Monica asks Cecilia to slap her in the face; Cecilia declines: 'I'd love to, but my lawyer said I can't do that anymore.'
jokes.setup: Monica, starstruck, asks for the ultimate fan experience: a slap in the face from the character famous for slapping
jokes.punchline: Cecilia would love to but has been legally prohibited — implying she has actually slapped fans (and perhaps cast members) for real in the past
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke that pays off multiple earlier threads. The earlier scene where someone called for ice after Cecilia's 'theatrical' slap now gets a legal backstory. 'I'd love to, but my lawyer said I can't do that anymore' is a devastating character line — it confirms Cecilia is genuinely violent and has been legally contained. Highly quotable, great character integration, and a perfect callback structure.

jokes.text: Monica provokes Cecilia by calling her a 'stupid bitch' to try to trigger a slap — 'You are so beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Cecilia has said she legally can't slap Monica; Monica, desperate for the slap, tries to provoke her
jokes.punchline: Monica calls Cecilia a 'stupid bitch' in an attempt to provoke a slap, then immediately covers with 'You are so beautiful' when it doesn't work
jokes.explanation: An excellent cringe escalation. Monica is so star-struck and desperate for the slap experience that she willingly insults her idol. The pivot from 'stupid bitch' to 'you are so beautiful' in the same breath is a perfect character moment — Monica's desperation overriding her social intelligence.

jokes.text: Joey reads how his character comes out of the coma: 'You get thrown from a horse into an electric fence.'
jokes.setup: Joey is excited to have lines — it means he's out of the coma; Cecilia is anxious about how it happens
jokes.punchline: The method of recovery is a horse-throwing into an electric fence — a completely ridiculous soap opera plot point delivered as medical fact
jokes.explanation: Classic soap opera absurdity gag. The specificity of 'thrown from a horse INTO an electric fence' is funnier than a vague medical miracle. Builds well on the brain transplant absurdity from earlier.

jokes.text: 'Jessica hates horses.' / 'After this, she's not gonna be crazy about electricity either.'
jokes.setup: Cecilia objects to the horse element because her character hates horses
jokes.punchline: Joey points out that after being thrown into an electric fence, her dislike of electricity will be even stronger — a logical but absurd extension
jokes.explanation: One of the stronger jokes in the episode. Joey's deadpan observation that surviving an electric fence will add electricity to the character's hate list is logically sound and structurally elegant. The delivery has to be perfect — casual, matter-of-fact — and the transcript implies exactly that. High economy, high quotability.

jokes.text: Ross tells Chandler and Monica to 'imagine me in a kilt' for the bagpipe performance preview
jokes.setup: Ross is about to perform a preview of his wedding bagpipe piece
jokes.punchline: 'Imagine me in a kilt' as a helpful instruction for context — implying he's not wearing one, so they have to do the costuming in their heads
jokes.explanation: A mild joke about Ross's earnest commitment to the bagpipe bit. The image of Ross in a kilt is moderately funny; the fact that he thinks the kilt is what's holding them back is funnier.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I can imagine you in a short plaid skirt and knee socks.'
jokes.setup: Ross says to imagine him in a kilt for the full effect
jokes.punchline: Chandler sexualizes the kilt suggestion with 'short plaid skirt and knee socks' — implying a schoolgirl fantasy rather than Scottish traditional dress
jokes.explanation: Chandler's dry, slightly bizarre redirect is in character. The specificity of 'knee socks' adds to the weirdness. Mildly funny — doesn't reach the heights of his best lines but is serviceable.

jokes.text: Ross: 'You wanna start telling secrets?' (threatening Chandler about the kilt-fantasy comment)
jokes.setup: Chandler has made a strange sexualized comment about Ross in a skirt
jokes.punchline: Ross's response implies he has compromising secrets about Chandler that he could share — a mild threat that also implies real dirt exists
jokes.explanation: A quick, decent bit of banter. The implied threat is mildly funny but doesn't go anywhere specific enough to land big.

jokes.text: Ross plays his bagpipe 'Celebration' performance — Monica and Chandler's reaction is 'No. No.'
jokes.setup: Ross has asked for a chance to perform and promised they can decide afterward
jokes.punchline: After his performance, Monica and Chandler's simultaneous, flat 'No. No.' is the whole verdict
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the bagpipe subplot. The performance happens (we hear it in the audience), and then the unanimous, minimalist 'No. No.' is funnier than any longer reaction would be. The economy of two words to devastate Ross is well-judged.

jokes.text: Joey performs the brain-transplant scene as Jessica Lockhart — 'Who are you? / What's the matter, Dina? Don't you recognize your own... mother?'
jokes.setup: The brain transplant storyline finally plays out on DOOL — Joey must now play Jessica Lockhart's personality in Drake Ramoray's body
jokes.punchline: The scene is played as genuine soap melodrama, but the absurdity of watching Joey perform a woman's character while being clearly a man in a hospital gown makes the whole sequence comedic
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the episode's main plot. The comedy is primarily visual — Joey performing feminine soap opera theatrics — which limits its impact on the page but would land well on screen.

jokes.text: 'I think that you're a better Jessica than I ever was.' / 'Of course not, but you were good.'
jokes.setup: Cecilia gives Joey a compliment about his Jessica performance
jokes.punchline: Joey's response is a perfectly immediate, sincere self-correction: 'Of course not, but you were good' — accepting the compliment's premise (he was better) but magnanimously giving her credit
jokes.explanation: A great Joey-specific joke. He hears 'you're better than her' and genuinely accepts it without false modesty, then charitably says Cecilia 'was good' — as if she was fine but he's better. His ego and his genuine sweetness collide perfectly in this line. The structure (the implied agreement + condescending grace) is excellent.

jokes.text: 'I got another job. A film in Guadalajara.' / 'The airport?' / 'No, that's LaGuardia.'
jokes.setup: Cecilia announces she's gotten a new film job in Guadalajara, Mexico
jokes.punchline: Joey thinks Guadalajara is an airport — confusing it with LaGuardia
jokes.explanation: A classic Joey stupidity joke that works exceptionally well. Confusing 'Guadalajara' with 'LaGuardia' requires just enough phonetic similarity to make the error believable, while being catastrophically wrong. The two-word correction 'No, that's LaGuardia' has perfect economy — Cecilia doesn't even bother being exasperated, just corrects. Very quotable, strong character integration. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: 'You could come visit. I bet you could own a few places down there.' / 'Oh, you know, I should probably buy a place in the city first.' / 'And I just got what you meant. That is tricky.'
jokes.setup: Cecilia uses the 'own the room' phrase figuratively — 'you could own a few places down there'
jokes.punchline: Joey initially takes it literally (real estate) before the metaphor lands — 'And I just got what you meant. That is tricky.'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the 'own the room' acting lesson. Joey's delayed comprehension — and his judgment that the metaphor is 'tricky' — is perfectly in character. The warmth of the scene makes this a sweet final Joey moment.

jokes.text: "Oh, you know, I should probably buy a place in the city first." "And I just got what you meant. That is tricky." "It's tricky."
jokes.setup: Joey told Cecilia she could 'own a few places' in Mexico (using the acting lesson phrase); Cecilia deflects by saying she should 'buy a place in the city first'
jokes.punchline: The 'own the room' metaphor comes back a third time, with Cecilia and her date both catching the double meaning and appreciating the 'tricky' wordplay
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the 'own' wordplay — the callback has become a running motif. By this point the audience is primed for it, and the shared recognition between characters ('I just got what you meant') is a nice way to close the loop on the running wordplay.

tmdb_overview: Joey's character on Days of Our Lives is awakened from his coma with a brain transplant from one of the show's most legendary characters. Ross practices the bagpipes for Monica and Chandler's wedding. Meanwhile, Phoebe and Rachel fight over a guy who left his cell phone in Central Perk.
insight: Solid character work elevates a 70-point episode built on escalating Joey absurdity.
